blocks.heading: Responsiveness rather than size
blocks.text:
Price elasticity measures how strongly quantity demanded or supplied responds to a change in the product’s own price. Comparing percentage changes makes the measure independent of whether quantities are counted in individual items or hundreds. A fall of ten units could be large for a seller initially selling twenty but small for one initially selling a thousand. The percentage change supplies the needed reference. Divide the percentage quantity change by the percentage price change; do not reverse the ratio.

Classify responsiveness by the coefficient’s magnitude. Elastic means above one: the percentage quantity response is larger than the percentage price change. Inelastic means below one: it is smaller. Unit elastic means equal percentage changes, giving one. Perfectly (also called absolutely or completely) inelastic demand has a coefficient of zero: quantity does not change at all when price changes, and the demand curve is a vertical line. Perfectly elastic demand has a coefficient of infinity: at one price buyers take any quantity, but any rise above that price makes quantity demanded fall to zero, and the curve is a horizontal line. Most products lie between these extremes. Merely inelastic demand can still change quantity; it is not necessarily perfectly inelastic. These categories describe responsiveness over the relevant change and under the stated conditions. They do not mean that a whole product category has one unchanging coefficient in every market and time period. Use evidence about price and quantity rather than guessing the classification from whether the price looks expensive.

blocks.heading: Demand elasticity on a diagram
blocks.text:
Assume straight demand lines and unchanged other demand conditions. A shop sells 100 packets a week each of maize meal and one brand of crisps at N$20. Both prices rise 50 per cent, to N$30. Maize meal sales fall 25 per cent, to 75 packets: PED is −0.5, inelastic. Crisps sales fall 75 per cent, to 25 packets: PED is −1.5, elastic. Few close substitutes can make demand less elastic; competing brands can make it more elastic.

![Demand elasticity diagram](diagrams/item-6145-3.3-019-proc-answer.png)

From that point the flatter curve is more elastic over this change. With different scales or starting points, steepness alone does not show elasticity, which also varies along a straight demand line.

blocks.heading: Supply elasticity on a diagram
blocks.text:
Supply works the same way. Two workshops each make 50 chairs a month at N$400. The price rises 50 per cent, to N$600. Workshop A, with unused machines, raises output 80 per cent, to 90 chairs: PES is 1.6, elastic. Workshop B, near capacity, reaches 60 chairs, 20 per cent more: PES is 0.4, inelastic.

![Supply elasticity diagram](diagrams/item-6145-3.3-020-proc-answer.png)

A vertical supply curve is perfectly inelastic (PES 0), a horizontal one perfectly elastic, and a straight supply line through the origin unit elastic (PES 1) at every point.

blocks.heading: Applying demand responsiveness
blocks.text:
Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. It is the money received from sales before costs are subtracted, so it is not profit. When demand is price inelastic for the relevant change, raising price increases total revenue because the quantity sold falls proportionately less than price rises. For price elastic demand the loss of quantity can instead outweigh the higher price, reducing revenue. Unit elasticity means equal proportional responsiveness. A price cut works the other way. If demand is elastic, the quantity sold rises proportionately more than price falls, so total revenue increases. If demand is inelastic, the quantity sold rises proportionately less, so total revenue falls. If demand is unit elastic, total revenue stays about the same. A firm wanting more revenue should therefore raise price where demand is inelastic and lower it where demand is elastic. In a numerical example, check by calculating the revenue from both price-quantity pairs. Perfectly inelastic demand has no quantity response over the assumed change, but that is a special case rather than a description of most ordinary products.

Consider a stall increasing price from N$20 to N$22 while weekly sales fall from 100 to 95. Revenue moves from N$2,000 to N$2,090. Using initial values, price rises 10 percent and quantity falls 5 percent, giving demand elasticity magnitude 0.5, inelastic. The revenue increase is N$90; costs have not been supplied, so a profit conclusion would be unsupported. A different sales response could reverse the conclusion. The example demonstrates why a price rise alone is not a complete pricing argument. A firm needs evidence about the relevant buyers and should consider whether their response changes as they find alternatives over time.

blocks.heading: Factors behind responsiveness
blocks.text:
Close alternatives can make demand more price responsive because buyers can switch when one product becomes dearer. A necessity with few substitutes may have less responsive demand. Budget share can matter: a large expense creates more incentive to search for alternatives than a very small one. Adjustment takes time, so people may have greater ability to change habits or equipment in the longer term. These factors support a reasoned tendency rather than a guaranteed coefficient. A named product without case evidence is insufficient to establish a precise elasticity value.

Supply responsiveness depends on how easily producers can alter the amount offered. Spare capacity, available inputs and inventories can support a faster response. Production requiring long growing or construction periods may be difficult to expand immediately. A workshop with unused machines may offer substantially more after a price rise; a harvest already determined by the season may change little in the immediate period. The distinction is quantity response to own price, not a supply shift caused by new technology. Price changes move along the relevant relationship; changes in production conditions can alter that relationship. Keep the comparison period clear when applying either concept.

blocks.heading: Interpreting a calculated ratio
blocks.text:
An elasticity coefficient is a ratio, not a percentage. If quantity changes by 12 percent and price by 8 percent, dividing gives a magnitude of 1.5. The percentage signs belong to the changes being compared, not to the final coefficient. Saying elasticity is 1.5 percent would mislabel it. A coefficient of 0.5 means the proportionate quantity response is half the proportionate price change, not that quantity is half a unit or price is fifty cents.

Use a consistent reference basis. These worked examples use initial price and quantity as their bases, and prompts state that convention. If a question gives percentage changes directly, divide those percentages rather than calculating another percentage from the coefficient. If the price change is zero, the simple ratio has a zero denominator and cannot provide an ordinary numerical coefficient. Explain the missing information rather than invent a result. This topic links to market forces in 3.2 and pricing policies in 3.5: responsiveness helps explain the effect of a price decision, while demand and supply shifts explain changes in the underlying market conditions. A comparison should name both the percentage response and the underlying side of the market. Two coefficients may have the same numerical value while describing different economic agents. Evidence about buyers cannot be silently substituted for evidence about producers.
